explanations.explanation: Compassion it is. Verse 1 says, "For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob; once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land." (Isaiah 14:1) Look at where the chapter starts. Before any song about the king of Babylon, it opens with the LORD's compassion for Jacob.

Vengeance is a fair guess, since this chapter gets heavy for the king of Babylon later on. But the first line is about Jacob, and it says, "For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob…" (Isaiah 14:1). The song against the king doesn't start until verse 4. So the chapter opens with compassion first.

Anger does show up in this chapter, but it belongs to the oppressor. Verse 6 says the staff of the wicked struck the peoples in anger (Isaiah 14:6). For Jacob, Isaiah uses a different word: "For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob…" (Isaiah 14:1). Two sides, two very different words.

True, and the words are plain: "once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land." (Isaiah 14:1) Those two words, "once again," are doing a LOT of work. Chosen and settled, both in one verse.

It's True, and the verse says so directly: "once again He will choose Israel and settle them in their own land." (Isaiah 14:1) Nothing in that line takes it back or adds a catch. The LORD chooses, and the LORD settles. Easy to second-guess a line this good.

It's False, though I see the pull of that guess. Verse 1 says, "The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob." (Isaiah 14:1) So nobody is held at the gate. The words are "join" and "unite."
False. Verse 1 says, "The foreigner will join them and unite with the house of Jacob." (Isaiah 14:1) Join and unite, not kept away. That's about as far from a locked door as two words can get.

Isaiah 14:2 says, "They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors." The ones who held Israel will be the ones held. I can picture the captors' faces: "Wait, who's holding the keys now?!" That's my line, not Isaiah's.

Silver doesn't come up anywhere in these verses. Isaiah 14:2 says, "They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors." So instead of a payment, the roles turn around. A bill would have been a lot quieter.

Verse 2 doesn't say anything about sending them off empty. It says, "They will make captives of their captors and rule over their oppressors." (Isaiah 14:2) That's more than just letting the captors walk away. The captors end up on the other side of the line.

Contempt is the word. Verse 4 says, "you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon…" (Isaiah 14:4). And the song begins, "How the oppressor has ceased, and how his fury has ended!" It's sung on the day the LORD gives rest from pain and torment (Isaiah 14:3).

Mourning would fit a sad day, but verse 4 names a different song: "you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon…" (Isaiah 14:4). It comes on the day the LORD gives rest from pain and torment (Isaiah 14:3). So it's sung by people who have been given rest.

Thanks is a nice thought, and verse 7 does say the earth breaks out in song (Isaiah 14:7). But the song Isaiah names in verse 4 is "this song of contempt against the king of Babylon…" (Isaiah 14:4). The word is contempt, and it's aimed at the king.

The LORD. Verse 5 says, "The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers." (Isaiah 14:5) A staff and a scepter are what rulers hold in their hands. In this line, the LORD is the One who breaks them, and no army is named.

Pharaoh isn't named anywhere in this song. Verse 5 says, "The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers." (Isaiah 14:5) The answer is right there on the page. Pharaoh just isn't in this verse.

The king of Assyria isn't named in this song either. Verse 5 says, "The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers." (Isaiah 14:5) The One doing the breaking is the LORD. No human king gets the credit here.

Rage. Verse 6 says the staff "subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution." (Isaiah 14:6) Look at the words around it: "unceasing blows" and "relentless." That's a long stretch of pain with no pause button.

Mercy is the opposite of what verse 6 describes. It says the staff "subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution." (Isaiah 14:6) There's nothing merciful about "unceasing blows." The word is rage.
Wisdom sounds calm, and verse 6 is not calm. It says the staff "subdued the nations in rage with relentless persecution." (Isaiah 14:6) Rage, not wisdom. And relentless means it just kept going.

It's False, and I understand the guess, since this passage has some heavy parts. Verse 7 says, "All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song." (Isaiah 14:7) So the earth breaks out in song, not weeping. Peace and rest come first, and then the music.
False. Verse 7 says, "All the earth is at peace and at rest; they break out in song." (Isaiah 14:7) Not weeping, singing. The whole earth ends up in a sing-along, and nobody needed a rehearsal.

"Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us." That's what the cypresses and cedars say in verse 8 (Isaiah 14:8). If I were a cedar, I think I'd be cheering too, with a whole lot of branch waving. The woodcutter just isn't coming.

explanations.answer: The rain has finally come back
explanations.explanation: Rain isn't in the trees' words. Verse 8 gives what they say: "Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us." (Isaiah 14:8) Nobody is talking about the weather. It's about a woodcutter who isn't coming.

explanations.answer: Their roots have room to grow
explanations.explanation: Roots and room to grow are a nice thought, but they aren't what the trees say. Verse 8 has them say, "Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us." (Isaiah 14:8) What they're glad about is that the woodcutter stays away.

The rulers of the earth. Verse 9 says Sheol stirs the spirits of the dead to greet him, and those are all the rulers of the earth (Isaiah 14:9). It also says Sheol makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones. So the welcome comes from other rulers.

Prophets aren't mentioned in verse 9. It says Sheol stirs the spirits of the dead to greet him, and those are all the rulers of the earth (Isaiah 14:9). So the ones greeting him are rulers, not prophets. That's the answer the song gives.

Angels aren't named in verse 9. It says Sheol stirs the spirits of the dead to greet him, and those are all the rulers of the earth (Isaiah 14:9). So the ones rising to meet him are rulers. The song doesn't bring in heaven here.
It's False. Verse 9 says Sheol "makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones." (Isaiah 14:9) So the kings rise. Staying seated is the opposite of what the verse describes.

False. Verse 9 says Sheol "makes all the kings of the nations rise from their thrones." (Isaiah 14:9) They don't stay seated. They get up. Getting out of a throne is not a small thing for a king, I'd guess.

explanations.answer: You have become weak like us
explanations.explanation: "You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!" That's what they say in verse 10 (Isaiah 14:10). The ones who rose to meet him tell him he is weak now, just like them. It's a very plain thing to say.

explanations.answer: You will rule over us here
explanations.explanation: Ruling isn't what they say. Verse 10 has them answer, "You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!" (Isaiah 14:10) The word is "weak," not "ruler." They say he has become like them.

explanations.answer: You are stronger than us all
explanations.explanation: Stronger is the opposite of what they say. Verse 10 has them answer, "You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!" (Isaiah 14:10) The word is "weak." They tell him he is like them now.

Destroyer. Verse 12 says, "You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations." (Isaiah 14:12) The same verse opens with "How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn!" Those are the names the song uses for the one it is singing to.

Defender is the opposite of the title in verse 12. It says, "You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations." (Isaiah 14:12) Someone who guards nations doesn't get that name. The song's word for him is destroyer.

A shepherd looks after a flock, and verse 12 calls him something else: "You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations." (Isaiah 14:12) The song doesn't call him a shepherd anywhere. The title it gives him is destroyer.

Throne. Verse 13 says, "I will raise my throne above the stars of God." (Isaiah 14:13) The song says he said it "in your heart," so it was said inside. Then the plan keeps climbing: sit on the mount of assembly, in the far reaches of the north.
A banner is a good guess for a king, but verse 13 says, "I will raise my throne above the stars of God." (Isaiah 14:13) The word is throne. Not a flag, a seat.
An altar isn't in this verse. Verse 13 says, "I will raise my throne above the stars of God." (Isaiah 14:13) What he plans to lift up is a throne. The seat of power is what he wants raised.

explanations.answer: To make himself like the Most High
explanations.explanation: "I will make myself like the Most High." That's the last "I will" in verse 14 (Isaiah 14:14). Those "I wills" in verses 13 and 14 just keep coming. I think this one is the biggest of them all.

explanations.answer: To make peace with every nation
explanations.explanation: Peace with every nation isn't in his plans. The last "I will" in verse 14 is "I will make myself like the Most High." (Isaiah 14:14) Everything before it is about him going up, ascending, raising and sitting (Isaiah 14:13). It's all about him.

explanations.answer: To build a temple for the LORD
explanations.explanation: No temple shows up in his plans. Verse 14 ends with "I will make myself like the Most High." (Isaiah 14:14) Notice that every "I will" is about him. None of them is about building anything for the LORD.

explanations.answer: The lowest depths of the Pit
explanations.explanation: "But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit." (Isaiah 14:15) He said up, up, up, and the song says down. He wanted above the clouds and gets the lowest depths.

The sea isn't mentioned in verse 15. It says, "But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit." (Isaiah 14:15) You did land on the right direction, though: down. It's just not the sea.

The Valley of Hinnom isn't named in this verse. It says, "But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit." (Isaiah 14:15) The direction is down, just like you guessed. The place the song names is the Pit.

explanations.answer: Is this the man who shook the earth
explanations.explanation: "Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble…" (Isaiah 14:16) Those who see him are staring and pondering, and this is the question they ask. I think it's the kind of question you ask when you can hardly believe what you're looking at.

explanations.answer: Is this the man who healed the land
explanations.explanation: Healing isn't in their question. They ask, "Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble…" (Isaiah 14:16) And verse 17 goes on with "who turned the world into a desert and destroyed its cities…" (Isaiah 14:17). That's the opposite of healing.

explanations.answer: Is this the man who built our cities
explanations.explanation: Building cities isn't what they ask. Verse 17 says he "destroyed its cities…" (Isaiah 14:17). Their question is, "Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble…" (Isaiah 14:16) So the people remember him for shaking things, not building them.

It's False. Verse 17 describes him as the one "who refused to let the captives return to their homes?" (Isaiah 14:17) So the people remember someone who kept the door shut. The word in the verse is "refused."
False. Verse 17 describes him as the one "who refused to let the captives return to their homes?" (Isaiah 14:17) Refused, not allowed. That's how they remember him.

explanations.answer: He is cast out of his grave
explanations.explanation: He is cast out of his grave. Verse 18 says all the kings of the nations lie in state, each in his own tomb, and then verse 19 says, "But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch…" (Isaiah 14:18-19) I think this one is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly. The other kings rest in tombs, and he does not.

explanations.answer: He is buried with great honor
explanations.explanation: Honor isn't what verse 19 says. It says, "But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch…" (Isaiah 14:19) The kings in verse 18 each lie in their own tomb. That "But" marks the contrast with them.

explanations.answer: He is laid among his fathers
explanations.explanation: Lying in a tomb is what the other kings get: "All the kings of the nations lie in state, each in his own tomb." (Isaiah 14:18) The king of Babylon is not laid among them. Verse 19 says, "But you are cast out of your grave like a rejected branch…" (Isaiah 14:19).

explanations.answer: He destroyed his land and slaughtered his people
explanations.explanation: Verse 20 says, "You will not join them in burial, since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people." (Isaiah 14:20) The reason is given right there in the verse. It's a heavy line, and I'll leave it just as it is.

explanations.answer: He never built a tomb for himself
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't say anything about a tomb he failed to build. Verse 20 gives the reason: "since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people." (Isaiah 14:20) That's the reason the song states. It's a heavy line, so I'll leave it plain.

explanations.answer: His own sons refused to bury him
explanations.explanation: His sons refusing isn't in the verse. Verse 20 says, "You will not join them in burial, since you have destroyed your land and slaughtered your own people." (Isaiah 14:20) The reason is what he did to his land and his people. It's a heavy line, and I'll leave it as it is.

It's False. Verse 21 says, "They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities." (Isaiah 14:21) This is a heavy verse, and the same verse gives its reason: "for the iniquities of their forefathers." I'll leave the weight of it as it is.

False. Verse 21 says, "They will never rise up to possess a land or cover the earth with their cities." (Isaiah 14:21) This is a heavy verse, and it gives its reason too: "for the iniquities of their forefathers." I'll just leave it plain.

True. The LORD says, "I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity," (Isaiah 14:22). Those are His own words, and He says them with "declares the LORD." Name, remnant, offspring and posterity are all in that one line.

It's True, and the LORD says it Himself: "I will cut off from Babylon her name and her remnant, her offspring and her posterity," (Isaiah 14:22). Nothing in the verse softens it. Name, remnant, offspring and posterity are all named, and verse 22 ends with "declares the LORD."
Broom. "I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction," declares the LORD of Hosts. (Isaiah 14:23) A broom is a plain tool, and in this verse it's the LORD's own word. He says it Himself.

A sword does appear in this passage, in verse 19, where the slain are described as "covered by those slain with the sword" (Isaiah 14:19). But that's a different line. In verse 23 the LORD says, "I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction…" (Isaiah 14:23).
Fire isn't named in this verse. The LORD says, "I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction…" (Isaiah 14:23). The tool He names is a broom. Sweeping is the picture in this line.
